authors: Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA), HealthData@IE project (with Department of Health and Health Research Board)
title: Report on the findings of a readiness assessment of data holders in Ireland in relation to health data access body services (HealthData@IE Deliverable 8.12)
method: national readiness survey of 16 data holders covering 21 datasets (100% response rate), plus focus groups, analysed with descriptive statistics and content analysis, built around three use cases (influenza, diabetes, colorectal cancer)
outcomes: data holders' readiness for EHDS secondary-use obligations: unique identifiers, data linkage, anonymisation, data quality, information-management maturity
headline: Only 57% of surveyed datasets use the Individual Health Identifier and 48% the PPS number; a third do not link with other datasets at all, and only 38% use anonymisation techniques.
summary_plain: Ireland's health quality authority surveyed its main health data holders to see how ready they are for the new EU health data rules. Many are not ready yet: no common patient ID is used across them, data are often not linked, and few anonymise data, so a lot of work is needed before 2029.
quality: Early implementation baseline from a national authority; small, purposive sample of mostly well-established national collections; descriptive only, no counterfactual; single country.
interested_party: National body tasked with setting up EHDS health data access services; EU-funded project

title: Special report 02/2026: EU transport infrastructure - Further delays and some cost increases, but a reinforced governance framework is in place for the future (an update of ECA special report 10/2020)
venue: European Court of Auditors, Special Report 02/2026
method: audit follow-up of eight EU co-funded transport flagship infrastructures: inflation-adjusted cost re-estimation (2019 prices) and schedule tracking to November 2025, plus follow-up of 2020 recommendations
outcomes: cost overruns, delays, EU co-funding (largely CEF grants) for TEN-T megaprojects
headline: Real costs of the eight megaprojects rose a further 24% since 2020 (82% above original estimates), driven by Rail Baltica (+160%) and Lyon-Turin (+23%); they received €7.9 billion in additional EU grants since 2020, and the 2030 TEN-T core network deadline will not be met.
summary_plain: The EU auditors checked eight big EU-funded transport projects again and found they are even later and more expensive than five years ago. Together they now cost almost twice the first estimates, and Europe's core transport network will not be finished by 2030.
period_geography: 2020-November 2025; eight cross-border/national TEN-T projects (incl. Rail Baltica, Lyon-Turin, Brenner, Fehmarn Belt)
quality: Independent audit with transparent cost data; covers CEF-Transport co-funded projects rather than the CEF Regulation's own effect, and the projects predate CEF 2021-2027; descriptive, no counterfactual.

title: Annual report on EU Joint Undertakings for the financial year 2023
venue: European Court of Auditors, annual report on JUs (published 2024)
method: annual financial and compliance audit of all JUs: substantive testing of grant payments, extrapolated error rates, and tracking of member contributions against founding-regulation targets
outcomes: JU budget execution, private members' in-kind contributions vs targets, error rates in grant payments
headline: By end-2023 JUs had reached 94% of their Horizon 2020 member contribution targets overall but EuroHPC only 45%, with EuroHPC private members reporting just €18.4 million of in-kind contributions against a €420 million target; estimated average error rate for 2023 grant expenditure was just below the 2% materiality threshold.
summary_plain: The EU auditors signed off the joint undertakings' 2023 accounts, but found that private industry partners in some of them, especially the supercomputing one, are paying in far less than promised. Mistakes in grant payments were close to the acceptable limit.
period_geography: Financial year 2023; EU (11 JUs incl. those set up under Regulation 2021/2085)
quality: Independent audit with hard financial data; focuses on legality, regularity and contribution targets rather than research outcomes; earlier edition of the FY2024 report already listed.

authors: European Commission, Directorate-General for Research and Innovation (Unit G4, Common Missions & Partnerships Service)
title: Performance of European Partnerships: Biennial Monitoring Report 2024 on partnerships in Horizon Europe
venue: Publications Office of the EU, doi:10.2777/991766
method: monitoring report with descriptive statistics on 44 European Partnerships (incl. the Art. 187 JUs) from eCORDA grant data and partnerships' self-reported leverage and KPI data
outcomes: leverage of private/other funding, success rates, participation, KPIs of institutionalised partnerships
headline: Institutionalised partnerships (JUs, excl. KICs) show total direct leverage of 1.44 euro per EU euro but indirect leverage of only 0.20, which the report says means JU outcomes do not yet trigger substantial follow-on investment.
summary_plain: The Commission's own monitoring of its research partnerships finds that the industry-led joint undertakings bring in about 1.4 euros of partner money for every EU euro, but so far spark little further investment to take results to market.
period_geography: Horizon Europe 2021-2023 data; EU27 plus associated countries
quality: Rich administrative data but leverage figures are self-reported and early in programme life (report flags reliability caveats); Commission monitoring its own programme; descriptive.

authors: European Commission and Consumer Safety Network (national market surveillance authorities)
title: Summary results of the first product safety sweep of the Consumer Safety Network - compliance of online marketplace offers of childcare articles with the requirements of the GPSR
venue: European Commission / Consumer Safety Network, July 2025 (copy hosted by Spain's Dirección General de Consumo)
method: coordinated enforcement sweep (compliance audit): pro-forma checks of 1,741 childcare product listings on 47 online marketplaces (1,202 on five VLOPs), 1 April-15 May 2025
outcomes: display of manufacturer and EU responsible-person information on listings; marketplace registration on Safety Gate and contact points; responses to authority orders
headline: Only 52% of listings gave full manufacturer information (65% on VLOPs vs 24% on smaller platforms) and 68% full EU responsible-person information; only 53% of marketplaces had registered on the Safety Gate Portal and 64% had a consumer contact point; 252 orders were sent.
summary_plain: In the first EU-wide check under the new product safety law, national authorities looked at baby and childcare products sold online. Half the listings lacked required details on who made the product, and only half of the online marketplaces had registered with the EU's safety alert system as the law requires.
period_geography: April-May 2025; EU/EEA market surveillance authorities, 47 marketplaces
quality: Systematic official compliance measurement soon after the GPSR began to apply; sample chosen by authorities, not random; measures information obligations rather than product safety outcomes.
interested_party: Commission and enforcers reporting on their own enforcement action

authors: European Commission and national market surveillance authorities
title: 2026 product safety sweep shows improving compliance with product safety rules while some gaps remain
venue: European Commission, Daily News MEX/26/1802, 7 September 2026
method: second coordinated enforcement sweep (compliance audit): checks of nearly 1,700 childcare and gym product listings on 35 online marketplaces, May-July 2026, compared with 2025 sweep
outcomes: marketplace registration on Safety Gate, consumer contact points, completeness of product safety information on listings
headline: 91% of marketplaces had registered on the Safety Gate Portal and named an authority contact point (up from 53% in 2025) and 100% had a consumer contact point (up from 64%), but only 58% of listings gave manufacturer, EU responsible person and product identification together; 560 orders were sent.
summary_plain: A year after the first check, online marketplaces have mostly caught up on the basic duties of the product safety law, such as registering with the EU's alert system. But four in ten product listings still lack key safety details.
quality: Repeat official measurement allows before/after comparison, but samples and product categories differ between years; only the Commission's announcement was seen, not a full report.
interested_party: Commission reporting on its own enforcement action

authors: Civil Liberties Union for Europe (Liberties), with 40 member and partner organisations
title: Media Freedom Report 2026
venue: Civil Liberties Union for Europe, April 2026
method: structured qualitative monitoring: country reports from 40 civil society organisations in 22 member states on common indicators, including EMFA implementation and follow-up of Commission rule-of-law recommendations
outcomes: national implementation of EMFA; media ownership concentration, public service media independence, state advertising, journalist safety
headline: In the first months after EMFA started to apply (August 2025), most of its provisions had not been incorporated into national law in the 22 countries covered; France had done nothing by December 2025, Bulgaria and Romania missed deadlines, and Hungary sued to annul the act, with only Slovenia adopting a new media law reflecting EMFA safeguards.
summary_plain: A network of civil liberties groups looked at 22 EU countries and found that the new EU media freedom law has so far changed little: most governments have been slow or reluctant to bring national rules into line, and media concentration and pressure on public broadcasters kept growing in 2025.
quality: Broad structured qualitative assessment, early in EMFA's application; no quantitative compliance index; contributors are advocacy organisations.
interested_party: Campaigning NGO network on media freedom and rule of law

authors: Bálint Barki, Gábor Polyák (Mérték Media Analysis Workshop, with Connect Europe)
title: Monitoring the implementation of the European Media Freedom Act: EMFA's Hungarian implications and impact on the Hungarian legal environment - Monitoring Report II
method: structured legal-compliance monitoring: article-by-article check of EMFA obligations on the Hungarian legislator, regulator (NMHH) and other bodies, plus review of the European Board for Media Services' activity
outcomes: Hungarian compliance with EMFA obligations (source protection, media merger assessment, ownership database, state advertising criteria, PSM governance)
headline: Three and a half months after EMFA became fully applicable, Hungary and its regulators had fulfilled none of their EMFA obligations and no preparatory work was under way; the European Board for Media Services and the Commission had taken no steps on Hungary.
summary_plain: Hungarian media researchers checked what Hungary has done to follow the new EU media freedom law and found nothing had been done, for example on protecting journalists' sources or reviewing media takeovers. EU bodies had not acted either.
quality: Detailed qualitative legal assessment for one high-risk country; no data analysis; authors from an organisation critical of the government's media policy.
interested_party: Media freedom NGO critical of Hungarian government media policy
